title: Building an Agentic Platform — Ben Kus, CTO Box

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's central subject is designing and implementing agentic architecture with directed graph orchestration, reflection, multi-model voting, and tool-based checking for enterprise data extraction. Box is an enterprise content platform and the use cases span enterprise document workflows and deep research over enterprise content corpora. The talk traces the journey from initial architecture through production challenges to agentic redesign, deployment, and incremental improvement. The talk assumes familiarity with LLM capabilities, agentic concepts, and enterprise system architecture. The content is a single-speaker conference talk by Box's CTO at the AI Engineer channel. summary: Ben Kus, CTO of Box, presents Box's evolution from traditional ML through LLM-based extraction to an agentic architecture for metadata extraction. Box operates an unstructured content platform with over 115,000 enterprise customers, two-thirds of the Fortune 500, and over an exabyte of data across hundreds of billions of files. Many enterprises' first AI deployment was with Box due to its security and data leakage protections. In 2023, Box launched generative AI features including QA, data extraction, and AI-powered workflows. The first version used OCR pre-processing plus single-shot LLM extraction, which initially performed remarkably well. However, customers pushed it with complex cases: 300-page lease documents with 300 fields, complex digital assets, risk assessments, and international languages. Challenges mounted including OCR brittleness, AI attention limits on many fields, lack of confidence scores from LLMs, and the inadequacy of LLM-as-judge approaches for enterprise accuracy. Box hit a despair moment realizing the architecture's fragility couldn't be solved by waiting for better models. The team controversially adopted agentic approaches over engineer suggestions to improve OCR or fine-tune models. The agentic routine intelligently breaks up field sets, performs multiple queries on documents, uses tools to double-check results (OCR, page images, multi-model voting), and employs LLM-as-judge with feedback loops telling the AI to try again. This architecture enabled incremental fixes—adding nodes or changing prompts—rather than full redesigns. Box extended the agentic foundation to deep research capabilities on enterprise content, using directed graphs for searching, planning, outlining, and processing. Key lessons include: the agentic abstraction layer is architecturally clean and separable from distributed system scaling concerns; agentic-first thinking should be cultivated in engineering teams; and agentic architecture should be built early when AI models could plausibly help. Box publishes MCP servers and supports agent-to-agent communication. Box is anti-fine-tuning, supporting multiple models (Gemini, Llama, OpenAI, Anthropic) and preferring prompts, cached prompts, and agentic design because fine-tuning is hard to maintain across model evolutions. Evaluation uses standard eval sets, challenge eval sets, LLM-as-judge, and human feedback. Everything is exposed via an agent API.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Box's Content Platform and Enterprise Focus
sections.summary: Ben Kus introduces Box as a 15+ year unstructured content platform serving 115,000+ enterprise customers including two-thirds of the Fortune 500, managing over an exabyte of data. Many enterprises' first AI deployment was with Box due to security and data leakage protections.

sections.title: Initial AI Deployment in 2023
sections.summary: Box began its generative AI journey in 2023, launching features including QA across documents, data extraction, and AI-powered workflows. The talk focuses specifically on data extraction from unstructured data.

sections.title: The Challenge of Unstructured Data in Enterprises
sections.summary: Approximately 90% of enterprise data is unstructured. For years, customers wanted better automation of unstructured data for querying, workflows, and search. The prototypical example is extracting key fields from contracts. Pre-generative AI IDP was a multi-billion dollar industry but required specialized models and was brittle.

sections.title: First Version: LLM-Based Extraction
sections.summary: Box's first approach used OCR pre-processing plus single-shot LLM extraction with prompt decoration. Off-the-shelf models from multiple vendors outperformed past specialized models. It was flexible across data types and performed well initially.

sections.title: Challenges with the Pure LLM Approach
sections.summary: Customers pushed with complex cases: 300-page leases with 300 fields, risk assessments, and international languages. OCR brittleness, AI attention limits on many fields, lack of LLM confidence scores, and LLM-as-a-judge inadequacy created mounting challenges for enterprise accuracy requirements.

sections.title: Despair and the Need for a New Architecture
sections.summary: Box hit a despair moment realizing the LLM architecture was fragile. Waiting for better models was insufficient. Engineers suggested improving OCR, adding post-processing, or fine-tuning, but these would lose the generality of the approach.

sections.title: Introducing Agentic Architecture
sections.summary: Box adopted agentic approaches with instructions, objectives, tools, secure access, memory, and directed graph orchestration. The team implemented LangGraph-style agentic routines with reflection, criticism, task separation, and field grouping while maintaining the same document-in, answers-out interface.

sections.title: Agentic Routine Details and Deep Research
sections.summary: The agentic routine intelligently breaks up related fields (e.g., parties and addresses), performs multiple queries per document, uses tools like OCR and page images to double-check results, and employs multi-model voting where models from different vendors disagree and resolve answers. LLM-as-judge provides feedback to try again rather than just labeling answers. This architecture enabled incremental fixes—adding a node or changing a prompt—instead of full redesigns. Box extended this foundation to deep research on enterprise content, using directed graphs for searching, relevance checking, outlining, planning, and processing, similar to how OpenAI or Gemini do deep research on the internet.

sections.title: Key Lessons Learned
sections.summary: Kus shares lessons: the agentic abstraction layer is architecturally clean and natural once adopted; agentic framework thinking should be separated from distributed system scaling thinking; agentic systems are easy to evolve (e.g., adding a summarization node to fix sloppy output); teams need to cultivate agentic-first and AI-first thinking; and building on the platform helps teams understand how to improve it for enterprise customers, including publishing MCP servers and enabling agent-to-agent communication. The overarching lesson: build agentic architecture early if AI models could plausibly help solve the problem.

sections.title: Q&A: API, Evaluation, and Fine-Tuning Stance
sections.summary: Box exposes agentic capabilities via an agent API. Evaluation uses standard eval sets, challenge eval sets for hard cases, LLM-as-judge, and human feedback, though enterprise privacy limits observability. Box is anti-fine-tuning because it is hard to maintain across model evolutions and multiple supported vendors (Gemini, Llama, OpenAI, Anthropic); the team prefers prompts, cached prompts, and agentic design, noting that next model versions usually improve on their own.
